## Overview

The Mro, also known as the Mro-cha, Mru, Murong, Taung Mro, Mrung, and Mrucha, are a subgroup of the Chin people living in the border regions of Myanmar, Bangladesh, and India. In Bangladesh, they reside primarily in Bandarban District and Rangamati Hill District in the Chittagong Hills. They also live in the surrounding hills and valleys of the Kaladan and Lemro rivers, and communities are recorded in the Chittagong Hills of southern Bangladesh. The sources give rough population estimates rather than a current census: around 20,000–25,000 people are located in the Chittagong Hills, while approximately 70,000 Mru live on the border of Myanmar with India and Bangladesh. The Mru language belongs to the Tibeto-Burman group of the Sino-Tibetan family. Their documented folk culture includes taungya cultivation, life-cycle rites, nat offerings, the Chiasotpoi ceremony, distinctive dress, and the ploong mouth-organ.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

Mru men wear Burmese jackets called *Kha-ok* and a cloth on the head that does not cover the top. These garments were bought from Indian hawkers. The lower body is covered by a self-made loincloth tied twice around the waist and passed between the thighs, with one end hanging at the front and the other at the back.

Before marriage, Mru women are described as topless, with the lower body covered by a short cloth skirt. The skirt is woven from yarn obtained from Indian merchants. During the Chiasotpoi rite, villagers put turbans on their heads while sitting on the body of the sacrificed cow.

### Architecture

In the Saingdin area, recorded in 1931, each hamlet contained between two and twenty bamboo houses. The sources describe small huts near streams during the New Taungya Cutting ceremony and bamboo arches erected over the village path while the village is closed for three days. After cremation, the remaining unburnt bones are kept for two or three months and then placed in a small hut constructed above the location where the body was cremated.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources document bamboo houses, bamboo huts, bamboo arches, bamboo tubes used to cook pieces of pork, baskets for vegetables and fruits, and a *khaung* pot. In taungya cultivation, spades are made with a long handle from an old taungya-cutting-dah that is no longer usable. Men use a *dah*, or dagger, in marriage exchanges, while a spear is also presented to the bride’s parents.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Some wealthy Mru women add a string of copper pieces to the string of beads around the waist. Women also wear silver earrings described as hollow tubes about three inches long.

## Music & performance

The principal documented Mru instrument is the *ploong*, a mouth-organ made from a number of bamboo pipes, each with a separate reed. It has two main components: a wind-chest and several pipes. The wind-chest is made from a calabash gourd, with a bamboo mouthpiece inserted through an opening in its neck. Its upper part is pierced with as many holes as there are sound pipes, usually from three to five.

The pipes are arranged in two rows. The left hand plays the rear row and the right hand the front row. Each pipe sounds when the small finger-hole on its side is closed. The sound pipes are cut from bamboo stalks, closed at the base, and fitted with free reeds whittled directly in the bark after the bark has been thinned. Wax is used both to fine-tune the pipe and to plug the joint between the pipe and wind-chest. A bamboo cap is placed over the other end to attenuate the tone and produce a more velvety sound.

The ploong is played during Chiasotpoi, where a full night of dancing and playing continues into the following day.

## Dance & theatre

The sources document a full night of dancing during Chiasotpoi, continuing into the next day. The ceremony is connected with devotion to a sacred spirit and the sacrifice of at least one cow, followed by a communal feast.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources describe annual agricultural rites connected with taungya cultivation. Before a new taungya is cut, villagers collectively buy two goats and gather two fowls from each household. After prayers for good health and abundant crops, the animals are slaughtered, their blood is sprayed over small huts and flowing water, and offerings are made to the nat. The village is then closed for three days, with bamboo arches placed over the path. The ceremony takes place once a year before cultivation begins.

When taungya fruits, vegetables, and paddy are ready for harvest, household members collect them and place them in a large basket and a *khaung* pot. A fowl is killed and its blood sprinkled over them. Another fowl is cooked with rice flour, salt, and ginger, and offerings are made to nats living in the staircase of the house. Villagers may harvest their produce after the ceremony.

At the end of the harvest, every household kills one or two pigs and cooks pieces of pork in a bamboo tube. The meat, rice, and *khaung* are taken to the taungya, where offerings are made to nats near the streams. A feast follows at home.

After a child is born, four short bamboos are placed beside the stream. A chicken is killed in honor of the nats, its blood is poured over the bamboos, and a prayer is made for the child’s well-being. At age twelve, boys and girls who follow the Krama faith participate in a coming-of-age ceremony.

Marriage negotiations involve the groom’s father, the prospective bride, and their families. The groom’s party brings three birds, a spear, and a *dah*; the spear and dagger are given to the bride’s parents, while the fowls are intended for the family to eat. The bride’s family cooks pork for the visitors. The sources also describe dowry arrangements and marriage contracted without parental consent.

At death, the body is placed in a coffin made of split colored bamboo and sometimes rugs and blankets, then cremated. The remaining bones are kept in the village for two or three months before being placed in a small hut. Death from contagious disease, especially small-pox or cholera, is followed by immediate burial without construction of the hut.

## Foodways

The sources describe rice and *khaung* as important foods in ritual and communal feasting. During the New Taungya Cutting ceremony, villagers cook the goats and make an offering with the meat and *khaung* before beginning the feast. During the Beginning of Taungya Harvest ceremony, rice is mixed with *khaung* and served with fowl after offerings are made to the nats. Neighbors are invited to eat the remaining meat.

At the end of the taungya harvest, pork is cooked in a bamboo tube and taken with rice and *khaung* to the taungya. After offerings are made, the villagers return home and feast on the remaining pork and *khaung*. During Chiasotpoi, rice beer or alcohol is served, and the cooked cow is shared by the villagers.

Marriage visitors bring fowls for the bride’s family to eat, while the bride’s family cooks pork for the visitors. The sources state that the two groups must not eat the food prepared for the other.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Mru claim that their ancestors lived at the source of the Kaladan River, although they are unsure when their people migrated to the region. Arakanese chronicles connect the Mru with the founding of ancient Arakanese city-states. One account says that the first king of Arakan married the daughter of the Chief of the Mru people and later founded Dhanyawadi. Another account describes the legendary King Marayu as raised by the Chief of the Mru tribe and marrying his daughter.

A legend tells of Nga Maung Kadon, who built barriers forming waterfalls in streams and tributaries connected to the Kalapanzin River to prevent a crocodile that had kidnapped his wife from escaping. A further Mru story explains why the cow has no upper teeth and why its tongue is cut during Chiasotpoi.

## Language & religion

Mru primarily speak the Mru language, a Mruic language of the Tibeto-Burman group of the Sino-Tibetan family. Dialects named in the sources include Anok, Downpreng, and Sungma. Mro-Khimi is described as a Kuki-Chin language of Burma, with varieties including Arang, Xengna, Xata, and Vakung. Traditionally, Mru had no written script, although some people could read and write Burmese or Bangla. The Mru language is written in Latin and the Mro alphabet, created in the 1980s by Man Ley Mru. In 1982, Kramadi Menle introduced the alphabet.

The majority of Mru follow Theravada Buddhism, while many self-reported Mru Buddhists also practice Animism. In 1984, Manlay Mro established the Krama faith, whose central text is the *Reyung Khiti*, or “Good Ethics.” Christianity is followed by a large fraction of the Mro in recent years, and a small community in Bangladesh has adopted Islam. Mru cosmology associates the sun with femininity and the moon with masculinity, while rainbows are understood as bridges by which Nats descend upon the earth.
